entries.title: Heavy loads build strength better than light loads
entries.take: For strength, heavy and moderate loads beat light loads, so most working sets should sit in the heavy to moderate range.
entries.body: A network meta-analysis of 28 studies in 747 healthy adults, all taken to failure, found muscle growth was similar across loads. Strength gains were larger with high loads (8 repetitions or fewer to failure) and moderate loads (9 to 15) than with low loads (over 15). High versus moderate was not clearly different. Light work still has a place for skill and recovery.
do: Keep most working sets on the competition lifts in the 1-8 repetition range.
Use light sets for warm-ups, skill work and easy days.

entries.title: Practise the lifts in competition style and hold four principles
entries.take: Strength in the squat, bench press and deadlift is partly skill, so the lifts themselves, done to competition standard, make up most of the training.
entries.body: This is coaching convention, not a trial result. Train squat depth, the bench pause and the deadlift lockout the way they are judged. Four principles apply to all three lifts: a stable base, full-body tightness before the bar moves, a bar path close to a straight line over mid-foot, and the same set-up every rep. Assistance exercises support the lifts and do not replace them.
do: Film your heaviest set of each lift every week, from the side.
Use the same set-up routine on warm-ups and on heavy sets.

entries.title: RPE with reps in reserve lets you pick the load by feel
entries.take: A set rated RPE 9 left one repetition in reserve and RPE 10 left none; the scale worked on all three lifts in powerlifters.
entries.body: The scale pairs effort with repetitions in reserve (RIR): RPE 10 is 0 RIR and RPE 9 is 1 RIR. In 29 lifters, experienced squatters rated a 1RM higher than novices, and bar speed fell as RPE rose. In 15 powerlifters, RPE at 1RM was 9.6 to 9.7 on all three lifts, and RPE tracked percent of 1RM closely (r = 0.88 to 0.91).
do: Rate each top set right after it ends, before looking at the bar speed or the numbers.

entries.title: Loading by RPE or bar speed works about as well as percentages
entries.take: Trials and a meta-analysis found no clear strength difference between autoregulated loading and fixed-percentage loading.
entries.body: A meta-analysis found no significant 1RM difference between autoregulated and standard percentage loading in resistance-trained people (mean difference 2.07 kg, 95% CI -0.32 to 4.46). In an 8-week trial of 21 trained men, RPE-based and percent-based loading both raised squat and bench press 1RM, and the gap between them was not significant. Both are valid ways to set load.
do: Use RPE when daily readiness swings; use percentages when you want a fixed plan to compare weeks.

entries.title: Velocity loss limits did not change strength gains in a large review
entries.take: Ending a set when bar speed has dropped by a set percentage is a valid way to cap fatigue; the threshold changed strength little.
entries.body: A meta-analysis of 19 longitudinal studies found the velocity loss chosen within sets did not change strength gains, while higher velocity loss went with more muscle growth. A second meta-analysis found thresholds of 25% or less gave slightly more 1RM strength (2.32 kg, 95% CI 0.33 to 4.31). Bar speed at 1RM differs by lift (0.23, 0.10 and 0.14 m/s for squat, bench and deadlift in 15 powerlifters), so each lift needs its own profile.
do: Record bar speed on your own lifts for several weeks before using a velocity cut-off.

entries.title: Strength does not need sets taken to failure
entries.take: Stopping sets short of failure gave similar strength gains to failure training, so heavy work can end with repetitions in reserve.
entries.body: A meta-analysis of 8 studies found non-failure training gave a 0.6 to 1.3% larger strength increase than failure training, a gap the authors judged unlikely to be meaningful. A later meta-regression found a negligible link between reps in reserve and strength gain, although muscle growth did show a negative slope with reps in reserve, meaning more growth nearer failure.
do: Stop heavy sets with 1-3 repetitions in reserve; a missed rep costs recovery and, on the platform, a lift.

entries.title: More weekly sets build more strength, with sharply diminishing returns
entries.take: Strength rises with weekly sets and with training frequency, but the gains flatten faster than muscle growth does.
entries.body: A meta-regression of 67 studies (2,058 participants) found strength gains rose with weekly set volume and with frequency, with diminishing returns that were more pronounced for strength than for muscle size. An earlier meta-analysis found high weekly sets beat low weekly sets (effect size 0.18), and a frequency meta-analysis found no significant effect once volume was equated.
do: Add sets only when progress stalls, and add them to the lift that is lagging.

entries.title: A small dose of heavy work can still raise a powerlifter's 1RM
entries.take: About 3 to 6 heavy working sets per lift each week was enough to expect strength gains in powerlifters over 6 to 12 weeks.
entries.body: A multi-part study (interviews, surveys and two interventions with 25 intermediate to advanced powerlifters) proposed a minimum effective dose: about 3 to 6 working sets of 1 to 5 repetitions per lift each week, spread over 1 to 3 sessions, at loads above 80% of 1RM and RPE 7.5 to 9.5, for 6 to 12 weeks. It describes a floor for busy periods, not an ideal.
do: Use this dose in busy or injured weeks, not as a long-term plan.

entries.title: Training days per week usually rise with level
entries.take: Beginners do well on 2 to 3 sessions a week; advanced lifters often spread the lifts across 4 to 6.
entries.body: This is coaching convention. Beginners can practise each lift two or three times a week with little fatigue. Intermediates commonly train 3 to 4 days, with each lift twice a week. In a survey of 117 Norwegian powerlifters that included world, European and national champions, the most common answer (58.1%) was 5 to 6 sessions a week, with the most common load at 71-80% of 1RM.
do: Add a session only when recovery between sessions is good and the lifts are improving.

entries.title: Planned variation beats a fixed routine for 1RM strength
entries.take: Periodised programs raised 1RM more than non-periodised ones, including when total volume was matched.
entries.body: A meta-analysis of 18 studies (81 effects) found periodised training gave larger 1RM gains than non-periodised training (effect size 0.43). A later meta-analysis of 35 volume-equated studies agreed for strength (effect size 0.31) but found no difference for muscle size. These trials were short, so the long-term picture in elite lifters is less clear.
do: Change volume and intensity on a plan, not at random.

entries.title: Linear, block and undulating plans differ little in trials
entries.take: No clear winner between linear and undulating models; too few trials exist to compare block models.
entries.body: Linear plans raise load week by week, block plans stack phases (volume, then intensity, then peaking), and daily undulating plans vary reps and load between sessions. A meta-analysis of 17 studies (510 participants) found no difference between linear and undulating for strength. A later one found a small edge for undulating in trained people (effect size 0.61, 95% CI 0.00 to 1.22) and could not compare other models.
do: Pick the model you will follow for a full cycle and judge it on your own logbook.

entries.title: Lifters taper for 5 to 10 days by cutting volume and keeping heavy singles
entries.take: Surveys report a short step taper: volume down about 40-50%, intensity kept high, last heavy squat and deadlift 7-10 days out.
entries.body: These are self-reports, not trials proving a taper works. In 364 North American raw powerlifters, a step taper over 7 to 10 days with 41-50% less volume was typical, with full rest about 2.8 days before the meet. A small trial of 19 athletes found 3 or 5 days of full rest kept lower-body strength; upper-body strength held at 3 days but not 5.
do: Cut volume sharply but keep the competition lifts and a few heavy singles.
Rest fully for the last 2 to 3 days before the meet.

entries.title: Most strength athletes deload for about a week every 5 to 6 weeks
entries.take: Deloading is common but little tested: athletes cut sets and load, keep frequency and exercises, and add reps in reserve.
entries.body: An expert Delphi (34 coaches began, 21 finished the third round) defined a deload as a period of reduced training stress to mitigate fatigue and promote recovery. A survey of 246 strength and physique athletes found all deloaded, typically for 6.4 days every 5.6 weeks, keeping frequency and exercises. No trial has yet shown the best length or timing.
do: Plan a lighter week roughly every 5 to 6 weeks, and move it earlier when joints ache and performance stalls.

entries.title: Low-bar squats lean forward and load the hips; high-bar squats stay upright
entries.take: Bar position changes the squat: low-bar uses more hip and back, high-bar more knee and quadriceps.
entries.body: A review of back squat biomechanics found high-bar squats showed more knee bend, less hip bend, a more upright torso and greater depth. Low-bar squats showed more hip bend and forward lean, with more erector spinae, adductor and gluteal activity. A systematic review of classic powerlifting research suggested low-bar squats generally let lifters move more weight.
do: Try each position for several weeks and keep the one you can repeat at competition depth.

entries.title: Build the bench from the setup: tight back, planted feet, paused bar
entries.take: A stable arch and tight upper back shorten the bar path and make the pause on the chest repeatable.
entries.body: This is coaching convention. Keep head, shoulders and buttocks on the bench and feet flat on the floor. Pull the shoulder blades together and down, grip with the thumbs around the bar, and lower under control to the lower chest. Pause until the press command, then press back over the shoulders. Wider grips shorten the range, but federations cap grip width, so check the rulebook.
do: Pause every training rep on the chest for the same count as the meet.

entries.title: Sumo and conventional deadlifts load the joints differently
entries.take: Sumo uses a wide stance and a more upright trunk; conventional moves the bar farther and does more mechanical work.
entries.body: In a video analysis of 12 sumo and 12 conventional lifters at a national championship, sumo lifters used a wider stance (70 cm against 32 cm; about 28 against 13 in), turned the feet out more and kept a more upright trunk. Bar distance, mechanical work and predicted energy cost were about 25 to 40% greater for conventional. The study did not test which style lifts more.
do: Test both styles for a few weeks and keep the one that moves more weight with a steady back.

entries.title: Limb and torso lengths change which set-up suits you
entries.take: Proportions shift the best stance, depth and grip, so copy principles from top lifters and not their exact positions.
entries.body: This is coaching convention, not a tested rule. Long thighs relative to the torso tend to lean the squat forward and favour a wider stance. Long arms shorten the pull in the deadlift and lengthen the bench press path; short arms do the reverse. Use these as starting guesses and let filmed sets and bar speed decide.
do: Film from the side and compare two set-ups on the same weight before changing for good.

entries.title: Choose accessories for the point where the lift slows or fails
entries.take: Find where the bar slows, then train the muscles and positions that fail there with 1 to 3 exercises.
entries.body: A review describes the sticking point as the position in the range where difficulty rises disproportionately, and says working out its cause helps choose training. Powerlifters in a minimum-dose study typically used 1 to 3 accessory exercises per lift at RPE 7 to 9 and about 6 to 10 repetitions.
do: Film a slow or missed rep, locate the sticking point, then pick exercises that train that range.

entries.title: Bands and chains help trained lifters when loads are 80% of 1RM or more
entries.take: In a meta-analysis, variable resistance beat constant resistance for trained lifters at 80% of 1RM and above.
entries.body: A meta-analysis of 14 studies found variable-resistance training (bands or chains) beat constant resistance for maximum strength (effect size 0.80). In trained people the benefit appeared at 80% of 1RM or more (0.76) and not below (0.00). In surveys, 39% of 28 elite British lifters used bands and 57% chains, and 76.9% of 117 Norwegian lifters used variable resistance.
do: Add bands or chains to heavy work once the base technique is stable.

entries.title: Pick the class you can hold in training; move up when cutting costs lifts
entries.take: A lifter whose normal weight sits at a class limit can compete there with little cutting; large cuts are a reason to move up.
entries.body: This is coaching convention. Consider moving up when making weight takes more than a modest, gradual diet, when training quality drops in the weeks before weigh-in, or when you are growing into the next class anyway. An ACSM consensus statement on weight-category sports advises classifying athletes by preseason body composition and shortening the gap between weigh-in and competition.
do: Weigh yourself in the morning for several weeks and compare the trend with the class limit.

entries.title: Rapid weight cuts are common in powerlifting, and fluid loss costs strength
entries.take: Many lifters cut weight, mostly by fluid methods; fluid loss lowers strength and can harm health.
entries.body: Among 64 lifters at the 2018 IPF classic worlds, 83% cut weight (average 2.9% of body mass) and most reported negative effects on mood. In a survey of 321 lifters, 85.8% used rapid weight loss, and doctors and dietitians were rarely an influence. A meta-analysis of 28 manuscripts found hypohydration cut muscle strength by 5.5% on average. Extreme cuts can harm health; involve a sports dietitian or a doctor.
do: Do not use fluid restriction, sauna or laxatives to make weight.
Ask a sports dietitian or doctor before any planned weight loss.

entries.title: Short sleep lowers performance, with evening sessions hit harder
entries.take: A meta-analysis found sleep loss cut exercise performance by about 7.6% on average.
entries.body: Across 69 publications, sleep loss (6 hours or less in 24) lowered performance by a mean of 7.56% (95% CI -11.9 to -3.13), including strength tasks. Tests done in the morning were largely unaffected; those done in the evening were consistently worse. A systematic review of 17 studies found several nights of restricted sleep could cut force in compound lifts.
do: Protect sleep in the week before a meet and keep a normal bedtime.

entries.title: Injury rates look low, but most lifters report pain in the back, shoulder or hip
entries.take: Counted as time lost, injuries are infrequent; counted as pain that affects training, most lifters have one.
entries.body: A systematic review of 9 studies found 1.0 to 4.4 injuries per 1,000 training hours in powerlifting, with the spine, shoulder and knee most affected. A survey of 104 Swedish subelite lifters counted pain or impaired function and found 70% currently injured and 87% injured in the past year, mostly lumbopelvic, shoulder and hip; only 16% of those currently injured stopped training completely.
do: See a physio or doctor for pain that lasts more than a week, and adjust loads while it settles.

entries.title: Testing a true max every few weeks
entries.take: Frequent max attempts add fatigue and risk without adding much information.
entries.body: This is coaching convention. A true max is the heaviest single you can complete with legal technique. It is a hard, slow-to-recover effort, and a bad day gives a misleading number. Work from a training max set from recent RPE 8 to 9 sets, and keep true maxes for meets or planned tests every few months.
do: Test at a meet or a planned test day, not on impulse.

entries.title: Running percentages off an old or lucky max
entries.take: A percentage is only as good as the max behind it, so reset the number when strength changes.
entries.body: This is coaching convention. If the max is months old, the percentages are too light or too heavy, and a lucky one-off single makes the plan too hard to finish. Reps at a given percentage also vary between lifters, so use RPE alongside the plan and rebase when weights feel clearly off.
do: Rebase percentages after every cycle using your best recent set, not one lucky rep.

entries.title: Treating RPE as exact when most lifters misjudge reps in reserve
entries.take: People tend to underpredict reps left in the tank, so RPE is a rough guide that improves with practice.
entries.body: A meta-analysis of 12 studies (414 participants) found people underpredicted repetitions to failure by 0.95 reps on average, with wide variation. Accuracy improved when the prediction was made nearer failure, with heavier loads and in later sets. A set called RPE 8 may have been closer to RPE 9.
do: Calibrate by comparing your RPE with bar speed or filmed sets over several weeks.

entries.title: Cutting weight with fluid restriction in the last days
entries.take: Fluid restriction is a common but risky way to make weight, and it lowers strength and endurance.
entries.body: In the 2018 IPF classic worlds survey, fluid restriction after fluid loading was among the most common methods, used by about a third of lifters, alongside fasting and laxatives. A meta-analysis found hypohydration lowered muscle strength by 5.5% and muscle endurance by 8.3%. Where weigh-in is within about two hours of lifting, there is little time to recover.
do: Stay near your class limit with normal eating, and see a sports dietitian before any cut.

entries.title: Changing technique, equipment or exercises in the final weeks
entries.take: Late novelty brings soreness and risk with no time to adapt; keep the final weeks specific and familiar.
entries.body: This is coaching convention, and tapering interviews match it. Ten Croatian champions reported taper training that was highly specific, with assistance exercises removed and the same equipment as in competition. New Zealand elite lifters said poor tapers happened when they took a week or more off.
do: Wear competition gear in the last heavy sessions and drop new exercises.

entries.title: Repetitions possible at 90% of 1RM
entries.take: Typical maximum reps at 90% 1RM across exercises; the bench press averaged about 4.

entries.title: Repetitions possible at 70% of 1RM on the bench
entries.take: Typical maximum reps for the bench press at 70% 1RM; about 9 at 80% and about 4 at 90%.

entries.title: Spread in reps between lifters at 80% of 1RM
entries.take: The between-lifter standard deviation at 80% 1RM is 2.51 reps, so the same percentage gives different rep counts.

entries.title: Volume cut during a taper
entries.take: Surveyed North American powerlifters cut volume by 41-50%; a review of self-reported tapers gave about 40-45%.

entries.title: Last heavy squat and deadlift before a meet
entries.take: Most surveyed North American raw lifters did their final heavy squat and deadlift 7 to 10 days out; bench came later.

entries.title: Weekly working sets for a minimum effective dose
entries.take: A floor proposed for powerlifters: 3 to 6 sets of 1 to 5 reps per lift, at loads above 80% 1RM, for 6 to 12 weeks.

entries.title: Typical deload length
entries.take: Average deload length reported by 246 competitive strength and physique athletes, taken about every 5.6 weeks.

entries.title: Lifters who cut weight at the 2018 IPF classic worlds
entries.take: Cutters lost an average of 2.9% of body mass; most reported negative mood effects.

entries.title: Strength lost with hypohydration
entries.take: Average fall in muscle strength with hypohydration in a meta-analysis of 28 manuscripts; endurance fell 8.3%.

entries.title: Mean age of peak performance in world-class powerlifters
entries.take: From world championship results 2003-2017; powerlifters peaked about 9 years later than weightlifters.

entries.title: One-repetition maximum (1RM)
entries.take: The heaviest weight you can lift once with legal technique; the base for percentage programming.

entries.title: Working max (training max)
entries.take: A weight you can repeat on a normal day, often set below a true max, and used as the base for training percentages.

entries.title: Rating of perceived exertion (RPE)
entries.take: A 1 to 10 rating of how hard a set was; in strength training it is tied to how many repetitions were left.

entries.title: Repetitions in reserve (RIR)
entries.take: How many more clean repetitions you could have done when the set ended; 2 RIR means two more were possible.

entries.title: Velocity-based training (VBT)
entries.take: Setting load or stopping sets from measured bar speed, using a device that reports mean concentric velocity in metres per second.

entries.title: Daily undulating periodisation (DUP)
entries.take: A plan that varies rep ranges and loads between sessions within the week, such as heavy, medium and light days.

entries.title: Accessory exercise
entries.take: An exercise outside the three competition lifts, chosen to build a muscle or fix a weak point.

entries.title: Taper (peaking)
entries.take: A planned drop in training stress, mostly volume, in the last days or weeks before a meet so fatigue clears and strength shows.

entries.title: Deload
entries.take: A planned lighter week or block, with less volume or load, to clear fatigue between harder blocks.

entries.title: Sticking point
entries.take: The position in a lift where the bar slows most or where failures happen.

entries.title: Intensity zones as a percent of 1RM
entries.take: Common coaching zones with typical reps per set and their purpose; reps at a given percentage vary by lifter.

entries.title: RPE to reps in reserve chart
entries.take: RPE 5 to 10 matched to repetitions in reserve (RIR); 9.5 is a half step many lifters add.
rows: No repetition left; a true limit
No rep left, but you could add a little load
Two more possible; bar speed still decent
Three more possible; fast and controlled

entries.title: A 12-week cycle outline
entries.take: A common layout from base volume to meet week; adjust loads by RPE and your own recovery.
rows: More sets and reps at 65-80% of 1RM
Heavy doubles and singles at 85-95%; practise commands
Volume down 40-50%; last heavy squat and deadlift
Short, light sessions early; rest the last 2-3 days

lopez-2021.title: Resistance Training Load Effects on Muscle Hypertrophy and Strength Gain: Systematic Review and Network Meta-analysis
lopez-2021.support: Muscle strength improvement was superior for both high-load and moderate-load compared with low-load RT in overall and subgroup analysis (SMD, 0.60-0.63 and 0.34-0.35, respectively; P < 0.001-0.003), with a nonsignificant but superior effect for high compared with moderate load.

zourdos-2016.title: Novel Resistance Training–Specific Rating of Perceived Exertion Scale Measuring Repetitions in Reserve
zourdos-2016.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
zourdos-2016.support: Subjects reported an RPE value that corresponded to an RIR value (RPE-10 = 0-RIR, RPE-9 = 1-RIR, and so forth). ... Our findings demonstrate an inverse relationship between average velocity and RPE/RIR. Experienced squatter group exhibited slower average velocity and higher RPE at 1RM than NS.

helms-2016.title: Application of the Repetitions in Reserve-Based Rating of Perceived Exertion Scale for Resistance Training
helms-2016.support: A newly developed scale based on how many repetitions are remaining at the completion of a set may be a more precise tool. This approach adjusts loads automatically to match athlete capabilities on a set-to-set basis.

helms-2017.title: RPE and Velocity Relationships for the Back Squat, Bench Press, and Deadlift in Powerlifters
helms-2017.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
helms-2017.support: Fifteen powerlifters (3 women and 12 men...) worked up to a one repetition maximum. Rating of perceived exertion at 1RM on squat, bench press, and deadlift was 9.6 +/- 0.5, 9.7 +/- 0.4, and 9.6 +/- 0.5. The ACV at 1RM ... was 0.23, 0.10, and 0.14 m/second. Very strong relationships (r = 0.88-0.91) between percentage 1RM and RPE.

helms-2018.title: RPE vs. Percentage 1RM Loading in Periodized Programs Matched for Sets and Repetitions
helms-2018.support: Both loading-types are effective. However, RPE-based loading may provide a small 1RM strength advantage in a majority of individuals. Between-group differences were non-significant (p > 0.05). (1RMG n = 11; RPEG n = 10; 8 weeks.)

hickmott-2022.title: The Effect of Load and Volume Autoregulation on Muscular Strength and Hypertrophy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
hickmott-2022.support: No significant differences between autoregulated and standardized load prescription were demonstrated for 1RM strength (MD = 2.07, 95% CI - 0.32 to 4.46 kg). Velocity loss thresholds <= 25% demonstrated significantly greater 1RM strength (MD = 2.32, 95% CI 0.33 to 4.31 kg).

larsen-2021.title: Effects of subjective and objective autoregulation methods for intensity and volume on enhancing maximal strength during resistance-training interventions: a systematic review
larsen-2021.support: Fourteen studies met the inclusion criteria, comprising 30 training groups and 356 participants. All autoregulation training protocols resulted in an increase in 1-RM, from small ES to large ES.

jukic-2023.title: The Acute and Chronic Effects of Implementing Velocity Loss Thresholds During Resistance Training: A Systematic Review, Meta-Analysis, and Critical Evaluation of the Literature
jukic-2023.support: Eighteen acute and 19 longitudinal studies met the inclusion criteria. The choice of VL threshold does not seem to affect strength and muscle endurance gains whereas higher VL thresholds are superior for enhancing hypertrophy.

davies-2016.title: Effect of Training Leading to Repetition Failure on Muscular Strength: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
davies-2016.support: Eight studies were included in the meta-analysis. Non-failure training resulted in a 0.6-1.3% greater strength increase than failure training. ... the small percentage of improvement shown for non-failure training is unlikely to be meaningful.

robinson-2024.title: Exploring the Dose–Response Relationship Between Estimated Resistance Training Proximity to Failure, Strength Gain, and Muscle Hypertrophy: A Series of Meta-Regressions
robinson-2024.support: In all of the best-fit models for strength, the confidence intervals of the marginal slopes for estimated RIR contained a null point estimate, indicating a negligible relationship with strength gains.

pelland-2026.title: The Resistance Training Dose Response: Meta-Regressions Exploring the Effects of Weekly Volume and Frequency on Muscle Hypertrophy and Strength Gains
pelland-2026.support: 67 total studies of 2058 participants. Gains in muscle size and strength increase as volume increases. However, both best-fit models suggest diminishing returns, with the diminishing returns for strength being considerably more pronounced. ... strength gains increase with increasing frequency, albeit with diminishing returns.

ralston-2017.title: The Effect of Weekly Set Volume on Strength Gain: A Meta-Analysis
ralston-2017.support: Pre- versus post-training strength gains were greater with HWS compared with LWS [mean effect size (ES) 0.18; 95% CI 0.06-0.30; p = 0.003].

ralston-2018.title: Weekly Training Frequency Effects on Strength Gain: A Meta-Analysis
ralston-2018.support: When RT is volume-equated for combined multi-joint and isolation exercises, there is no significant effect of RT frequency on muscular strength gain. Volume-equated ... LF vs HF [mean ES 0.03 (95% CI -0.20-0.27); p = 0.78].

androulakis-2021.title: The Minimum Effective Training Dose Required for 1RM Strength in Powerlifters
androulakis-2021.journal: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
androulakis-2021.support: PL athletes ... can do so by performing ~3-6 working sets of 1-5 repetitions each week, with these sets spread across 1-3 sessions per week per powerlift, using loads above 80% 1RM at a Rate of Perceived Exertion (RPE) of 7.5-9.5 for 6-12 weeks and expect to gain strength. ... 1-3 accessory exercises per powerlift, at an RPE in the range of 7-9 and ... ~6-10 repetitions.

shaw-2022.title: Contemporary Training Practices of Norwegian Powerlifters
shaw-2022.support: One hundred seventeen respondents met the inclusion criteria ... The most frequently reported (58.1%) category of training was 5-6 times per week ... The most frequently reported load used in training was 71-80% 1 repetition maximum. The majority of Norwegian (76.9%) powerlifters train with variable resistance.

swinton-2009.title: Contemporary Training Practices in Elite British Powerlifters: Survey Results From an International Competition
swinton-2009.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
swinton-2009.support: A 20-item survey was distributed to 32 elite British powerlifters ... 28 of 32. Results revealed that 39% of the lifters regularly used elastic bands and that 57% incorporated chains in their training.

williams-2017.title: Comparison of Periodized and Non-Periodized Resistance Training on Maximal Strength: A Meta-Analysis
williams-2017.support: The cumulative results of 81 effects gathered from 18 studies ... indicated that the magnitude of improvement in 1RM following periodized resistance training was greater than non-periodized resistance training (ES = 0.43, 95% CI 0.27-0.58; P < 0.001).

moesgaard-2022.title: Effects of Periodization on Strength and Muscle Hypertrophy in Volume-Equated Resistance Training Programs: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
moesgaard-2022.support: Thirty-five studies met the inclusion criteria. ... periodized resistance training has a greater effect on 1RM strength compared to NP resistance training (ES 0.31). ... UP in trained participants (ES 0.61, 95% CI [0.00, 1.22]). Meta-analyses of other periodization model comparisons were not performed, due to a low number of studies.

harries-2015.title: Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Linear and Undulating Periodized Resistance Training Programs on Muscular Strength
harries-2015.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
harries-2015.support: 17 studies satisfying the inclusion criteria. There were a total of 510 participants. The meta-analyses determined that there were no differences in the effectiveness of linear vs. undulating periodization on upper-body or lower-body strength.

travis-2021.title: Characterizing the Tapering Practices of United States and Canadian Raw Powerlifters
travis-2021.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
travis-2021.support: A total of 364 powerlifters completed a 41-item survey. A step taper was primarily used over 7-10 days while decreasing the training volume by 41-50% with varied intensity. The final heavy (>85% 1RM) back squat and deadlift sessions were completed 7-10 days before competition ... Complete training cessation was implemented 2.8 +/- 1.1 days before competition.

winwood-2026.title: Tapering and Peaking in the Weight Lifting Sports: A Systematic Review of Athletes’ Self-Reported Strategies
winwood-2026.support: All seven studies were rated high quality ... Taper length typically ranged from five to nine days ... taper phases characterized by a reduction in training volume of ~ 40-45%.

grgic-2017.title: Tapering Practices of Croatian Open-Class Powerlifting Champions
grgic-2017.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
grgic-2017.support: Ten Croatian open-class powerlifting champions ... training during the taper was highly specific, the assistance exercises were removed, and the same equipment was used as during competition.

pritchard-2016.title: Tapering Practices of New Zealand's Elite Raw Powerlifters
pritchard-2016.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
pritchard-2016.support: Eleven New Zealand powerlifters ... poor tapering occurred when too long (1 week or more) was taken off training.

travis-2022.title: The Effects of 3 vs. 5 Days of Training Cessation on Maximal Strength
travis-2022.support: Nineteen strength-trained athletes ... maximal lower-body strength can be preserved during 3 and 5 days of training cessation, but maximal upper-body strength is only preserved for 3 days after 4 weeks of strength training in athletes.

bell-2023.title: Integrating Deloading into Strength and Physique Sports Training Programmes: An International Delphi Consensus Approach
bell-2023.support: Thirty-four coaches completed the first round, 29 completed the second round, and 21 completed the third round. A consensus definition is proposed: 'Deloading is a period of reduced training stress designed to mitigate physiological and psychological fatigue, promote recovery, and enhance preparedness for subsequent training.'

rogerson-2024.title: Deloading Practices in Strength and Physique Sports: A Cross-sectional Survey
rogerson-2024.support: Competitive strength and physique athletes (n = 246) ... The typical duration of a deload was 6.4 +/- 1.7 days, integrated into the training programme every 5.6 +/- 2.3 weeks. ... training frequency would remain unchanged during deloads.

glassbrook-2017.title: A Review of the Biomechanical Differences Between the High-Bar and Low-Bar Back-Squat
glassbrook-2017.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
glassbrook-2017.support: HBBS is characterized by greater knee flexion, lesser hip flexion, a more upright torso, and a deeper squat. The LBBS is characterized by greater hip flexion and, therefore, a greater forward lean.

ferland-2019.title: Classic Powerlifting Performance: A Systematic Review
ferland-2019.journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
ferland-2019.support: A total of 16 scientific articles ... practitioners should prioritize a low-bar squat and a wide grip bench press because they generally contribute to moving greater loads.

escamilla-2000.title: A three-dimensional biomechanical analysis of sumo and conventional style deadlifts
escamilla-2000.support: 12 sumo and 12 conventional style lifters during a national powerlifting championship ... wider stance (70 +/- 11 cm vs 32 +/- 8 cm) ... Vertical bar distance, mechanical work, and predicted energy expenditure were approximately 25-40% greater in the conventional group.

kompf-2017.title: The Sticking Point in the Bench Press, the Squat, and the Deadlift: Similarities and Differences, and Their Significance for Research and Practice
kompf-2017.support: The sticking point is understood as the position in the range of motion of a lift at which a disproportionately large increase in the difficulty associated with continuing the lift is experienced.

lin-2022.title: Effects of Variable-Resistance Training Versus Constant-Resistance Training on Maximum Strength: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

burke-2021.title: ACSM Expert Consensus Statement on Weight Loss in Weight-Category Sports
burke-2021.support: Strategies to support safer practices include minimal competition weight classification based on preseason body composition, reductions in the period between weigh-in and competition, and prohibition of unhealthy weight loss techniques.

kwan-2022.title: Prevalence, Magnitude, and Methods of Weight Cutting Used by World Class Powerlifters
kwan-2022.support: 42 male and 22 female powerlifters ... 2018 IPF classic world championship. 83% cut weight losing an average 2.9 +/- 4.3% of body mass. Most lifters experienced negative changes in psychological state, with only 9% reporting never experiencing any negative effect.

nolan-2022.title: Self-Reported Prevalence, Magnitude, and Methods of Rapid Weight Loss in Male and Female Competitive Powerlifters
nolan-2022.support: Competitive powerlifters (n = 321) ... Prevalence of RWL was 85.8%, with an average RWL of 3.0 +/- 1.9% body mass. ... doctors (85.5%) and dieticians (63.0%) were reported to be 'not influential.'

savoie-2015.title: Effect of Hypohydration on Muscle Endurance, Strength, Anaerobic Power and Capacity and Vertical Jumping Ability: A Meta-Analysis
savoie-2015.support: A total of 28 manuscripts met the inclusion criteria. Hypohydration impaired overall muscle endurance by 8.3 +/- 2.3% ... muscle strength fell by 5.5 +/- 1.0% (P < 0.05) with hypohydration.

knowles-2018.journal: Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport

aasa-2017.support: 9 studies were included. The spine, shoulder and the knee were the most common injury localisations in both sports. ... 1.0-4.4 injuries/1000 hours of training in powerlifting.

solberg-2019.journal: International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance
solberg-2019.support: Peak age (mean [SD]) was 35 (7) y for powerlifters ... using results from powerlifting World Championships in 2003-2017.

nuzzo-2024.support: A total of 952 repetitions-to-failure tests, completed by 7289 individuals in 452 groups from 269 studies. (Text: at 90% and 70% 1RM, ~5 and ~15 repetitions; bench press ~4, ~9, ~14 at 90, 80, 70% 1RM; SD about the point estimate 2.51 repetitions at 80% 1RM.)
